extracted.intended_audience: writers of science fiction (aspiring and practicing), participants in writing courses
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for creating and exposing believable, narratively-useful worlds in science fiction—covering approaches (alternate vs fully imagined), verisimilitude, pacing of information, plausibility, and relationship to character and plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: World building as essential / 'another character'
rubrics_metrics.description: All fiction is building some kind of world, and with science fiction world building is of particular importance — it can be like another character in the story and can decide the plot in ways realist fiction may not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the world as a force that shapes plot and character; acknowledge that everyday actions (e.g., making a drink) may work differently and therefore reveal world details. Use exercises (describe morning rituals) to uncover distinctive rituals. Example/anti-pattern: assuming background details are the same as contemporary Western life leads to a flat, unconvincing world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose approach: alternate reality ('almost now') vs fully imagined world
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate realities are 'almost now' with slight changes; fully imagined worlds are constructed from the ground up (examples: Never Let Me Go / Watchmen vs Philip K. Dick's Mars story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your story needs recognisable, accessible anchors (grounding fantastical elements in familiar reality) or a wholly new cultural/physical system. Use recognisable elements to make fantastical aspects accessible. Antipattern: presenting fantastical elements without accessible anchors that orient the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude — give the semblance of the real
rubrics_metrics.description: World building should use verisimilitude so it isn’t outside the reader’s grasp: defined rules and an internal logic make the fantastical accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with familiar actions and gradually reveal how they differ; ensure the world obeys its own rules. Example: Philip K. Dick mixing everyday farming imagery with carnival ships on Mars. Scoring note: worlds that feel internally consistent rate higher on believability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal logic and limitations (avoid deus ex machina)
rubrics_metrics.description: There have to be limitations; if characters or systems can do anything (e.g., sudden magic or a deus ex machina), narrative tension collapses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define constraints (physics, technology, social rules) and use them to generate conflict. Example: 2001’s gravity hooks to handle upside-down walking. Anti-pattern: introducing unconstrained powers to solve problems cheaply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide and maintain a plausibility scale (hard vs soft SF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science fiction sits on a sliding scale from 'hard' (grounded in plausible science) to space opera/fantastical (science fits around drama).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose where your work sits (e.g., The Expanse/2001 vs Star Wars/Culture) and be consistent. If you aim for 'what could be', research plausibility; if you lean on drama, ensure internal coherence. Consistency increases reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise character and story over spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Character and plot must come first; world building should serve the human story rather than overwhelm it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid beautiful but empty surface detail that leaves characters feeling like mannequins (example: some Chris Foss covers). Use the world to deepen access to characters (objective correlative). Antipattern: spectacular world with flat, unengaging people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mundane, everyday details to ground the world
rubrics_metrics.description: Background rituals and ordinary acts (eating, making a drink) are critical to verisimilitude and make a place feel real (example: showing people eating in Wakanda).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include small, vivid cultural/ritual details that reveal how people live and what they value. These should be integrated, not merely decorative. Scoring note: worlds with convincing mundane detail feel more lived-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go deep into society and culture, not just visual gimmicks
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface-level visual invention (quirky props, gimmicks) can be shallow if it fails to convey how the society works; deeper exploration of social structures makes a world richer (contrast Fifth Element vs Iain M. Banks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop cultural, economic, political, and everyday systems where relevant. Avoid relying on surface oddities alone to indicate world depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter the world through character perspective (objective correlative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict the world as experienced by your characters; the world should be shown through their emotions, rituals and habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a character's point of view to reveal world details organically. Ask: what does this character notice and why? Example: showing how a desert culture treats water as respect rather than waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research real-world analogues and exaggerate appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use knowledge of real environments, cultures, or practices (e.g., nomadic tribes, Amazon survival) as a basis for believable extrapolation to fictional settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult experts or historical examples and then heighten elements for dramatic effect (e.g., Frank Herbert using North African/Middle Eastern nomadic models for Arrakis). This grounds plausibility while serving narrative needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid infodumps — reveal the world gradually and dramatically
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers must expose world information without resorting to long paragraphs of exposition; reading should discover the world as part of the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use techniques like a 'stranger-in-a-strange-land' POV, discovery scenes, action, and conflict-driven dialogue (avoid 'dead' expository dialogue). Release information through character reactions and stakes rather than flat explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the writer know more than the reader (iceberg principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer should contain a deeper, fuller understanding of the world than is revealed; readers should only see the tip of the iceberg.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave much unstated but consistent in the background. Give 'just enough' detail to trigger readers’ imaginations. Anti-pattern: telling everything explicitly, resulting in tedium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use unexplained oddities strategically (leave mystery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not everything must be explained; deliberate gaps can create mystery and disturbance (examples: unexplained 'frapped' drink; Alien’s calcified creature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow some phenomena to remain unexplained if it serves mood/tension. Balance is required: too many unexplained things can confuse; well-placed mysteries can be compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural estrangement — make genuinely different futures feel different
rubrics_metrics.description: When setting far in the future or in an alien culture, the reader should feel estranged; if it’s too comfortable it may fail to do its job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold back key cultural details initially to create estrangement, then reveal them to produce the sense of having visited a truly different place (example: Left Hand of Darkness). Manage readability so estrangement doesn’t lose the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance how much to withhold vs reveal (maintain narrative tension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how much information to release and when — balance is everything to maintain reader interest and narrative tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editing is where you calibrate this balance. Short stories tolerate more withholding because of single-sitting reading; novels may require different pacing. Use revisions to tune the amount of exposition and mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical writing process: have enough world to start, then discover more
rubrics_metrics.description: You should have a bit of an idea of the world before starting, but you can explore and discover details while writing; different writers need different amounts up-front.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-building without a story to use it. Create the amount of world 'bible' that helps you write, but stay focused on how the world will be used in the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cliché and find new, sensible ways to do familiar things
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on tired tropes (e.g., unexplained teleportation); instead invent solutions that make sense within your world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's acceptable to include implausible elements if they serve the story, but they should feel fresh and justified. Seek originality in how you implement genre staples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely in the genre to understand current practice
rubrics_metrics.description: To write convincing science fiction you need to read a lot of SF and be aware of what is happening in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with the genre helps avoid repetition and informs your choices about plausibility, tone, and world-building strategies. This is part of craft development rather than a one-off rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing as the tool to shape world exposure and plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing determines how much nuance the reader receives and how the world functions narratively; first drafts can be exploratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use revision to decide what world-detail to keep, what to trim, and how to pace revelations. Treat initial over-specification as material to be shaped rather than a final requirement.
